{{Short description|Refinement of perfect matching theorems}}

[[File:Graph deficiency.svg|thumb|upright=0.75|The '''deficiency''' of the set of red vertices {{math|''U''}} is the size of {{math|''U''}} minus the size of the set of all vertices that are [[Neighbourhood (graph theory)|neighbors]] of a vertex in {{math|''U''}} (the blue vertices)]]

'''Deficiency''' is a concept in [[graph theory]] that is used to refine various theorems related to [[perfect matching]] in graphs, such as [[Hall's marriage theorem]]. This was first studied by [[Øystein Ore]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Ore|first=Oystein|date=1955-12-01|title=Graphs and matching theorems|url=https://projecteuclid.org/euclid.dmj/1077466548|journal=Duke Mathematical Journal|language=en|volume=22|issue=4|pages=625–639|doi=10.1215/S0012-7094-55-02268-7|issn=0012-7094|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref name="lp">{{Cite Lovasz Plummer}}</ref>{{rp|17}} A related property is '''surplus'''.

== Definition of deficiency ==

Let {{math|1=''G'' = (''V'', ''E'')}} be a graph, and let {{math|''U''}} be an [[Independent set (graph theory)|independent set]] of vertices, that is, {{math|''U''}} is a subset of {{math|''V''}} in which no two vertices are connected by an edge. Let {{math|''N<sub>G</sub>''(''U'')}} denote the set of [[Neighbourhood (graph theory)|neighbors]] of {{math|''U''}}, which is formed by all vertices from {{math|''V''}} that are connected by an edge to one or more vertices of {{math|''U''}}. The '''deficiency''' of the set {{math|''U''}} is defined by:
:<math>\mathrm{def}_G(U) := |U| - |N_G(U)|</math>

Suppose {{math|''G''}} is a [[bipartite graph]], with bipartition {{math|1=''V'' = ''X'' ∪ ''Y''}}. The '''deficiency''' of {{math|''G''}} with respect to one of its parts (say {{math|''X''}}), is the maximum deficiency of a subset of {{math|''X''}}:
:<math>\mathrm{def}(G;X) := \max_{U\subseteq X} \mathrm{def}_G(U)</math>
Sometimes this quantity is called the '''critical difference''' of {{math|''G''}}.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Beckenbach|first1=Isabel|last2=Borndörfer|first2=Ralf|date=2018-10-01|title=Hall's and Kőnig's theorem in graphs and hypergraphs|journal=[[Discrete Mathematics (journal)|Discrete Mathematics]]|language=en|volume=341|issue=10|pages=2753–2761|doi=10.1016/j.disc.2018.06.013|doi-access=|issn=0012-365X}}</ref>

Note that {{math|def<sub>''G''</sub>}} of the empty subset is {{math|0}}, so {{math|def(''G'';''X'') ≥ 0}}.

== Deficiency and matchings ==
{{See also|Tutte's theorem on perfect matchings|Tutte–Berge formula}}

If def(''G;''X) = 0, it means that for all subsets ''U'' of ''X'', |N<sub>''G''</sub>(''U'')| ≥ |''U''|. Hence, by [[Hall's marriage theorem]], ''G'' admits a [[perfect matching]].

In contrast, if def(''G;''X) > 0, it means that for some subsets ''U'' of ''X'', |N<sub>''G''</sub>(''U'')| < |''U''|. Hence, by the same theorem, ''G'' does not admit a [[perfect matching]]. Moreover, using the notion of deficiency, it is possible to state a quantitative version of Hall's theorem: 
{{math theorem|math_statement=Every bipartite graph ''G'' = (''X''+''Y'', ''E'') admits a matching in which at most def(''G'';''X'') vertices of ''X'' are unmatched.}}

''Proof''. Let ''d'' = def(G;X). This means that, for every subset ''U'' of ''X'', |N<sub>''G''</sub>(''U'')| ≥ |''U''|-''d''. Add ''d'' dummy vertices to ''Y'', and connect every dummy vertex to all vertices of ''X''. After the addition, for every subset ''U'' of ''X'', |N<sub>''G''</sub>(''U'')| ≥ |''U''|. By Hall's marriage theorem, the new graph admits a matching in which all vertices of ''X'' are matched. Now, restore the original graph by removing the ''d'' dummy vertices; this leaves at most ''d'' vertices of ''X'' unmatched.

This theorem can be equivalently stated as:<ref name="lp" />{{rp|17}} 
:<math>\nu(G) = |X| - \operatorname{def}(G;X),</math>
where ''ν''(''G'') is the size of a [[Maximum cardinality matching|maximum matching]] in ''G'' (called the ''matching number'' of ''G'').

== Properties of the deficiency function ==
In a [[bipartite graph]] ''G'' = (''X''+''Y'', ''E''), the deficiency function is a [[Supermodular function|supermodular set function]]: for every two subsets ''X''<sub>1</sub>, ''X''<sub>2</sub> of ''X'':<ref name="lp" />{{rp|Lem.1.3.2}}<blockquote><math>\operatorname{def}_G(X_1\cup X_2) + \operatorname{def}_G(X_1\cap X_2)  \geq \operatorname{def}_G(X_1) +  \operatorname{def}_G(X_2)</math></blockquote>A '''tight''' subset is a subset of ''X'' whose deficiency equals the deficiency of the entire graph (i.e., equals the maximum). The intersection and union of tight sets are tight; this follows from properties of upper-bounded supermodular set functions.<ref name="lp" />{{rp|Lem.1.3.3}}

In a non-bipartite graph, the deficiency function is, in general, not supermodular.

== Strong Hall property ==
A graph ''G'' has the '''Hall property''' if Hall's marriage theorem holds for that graph, namely, if ''G'' has either a perfect matching or a vertex set with a positive deficiency. A graph has the '''strong Hall property''' if def(G) = |V| - 2 ν(G). Obviously, the strong Hall property implies the Hall property. Bipartite graphs have both of these properties, however there are classes of non-bipartite graphs that have these properties.

In particular, a graph has the strong Hall property if-and-only-if it is '''stable''' - its maximum matching size equals its maximum [[fractional matching]] size.<ref name=":0" />

== Surplus ==
The '''surplus''' of a subset ''U'' of ''V'' is defined by:<blockquote>sur<sub>G</sub>(''U'') := |N<sub>''G''</sub>(''U'')| − |''U''| = −def<sub>G</sub>(''U'')</blockquote>The surplus of a graph ''G'' w.r.t. a subset ''X'' is defined by the minimum surplus of ''non-empty'' subsets of ''X'':<ref name="lp" />{{rp|19}} <blockquote>sur(''G;''X) := min [''U'' a non-empty subset of ''X''] sur<sub>G</sub>(''U'')</blockquote>Note the restriction to non-empty subsets: without it, the surplus of all graphs would always be 0. Note also that:<blockquote>def(G;X) = max[0, −sur(''G;'' X)]</blockquote>In a bipartite graph ''G'' = (''X''+''Y'', ''E''), the surplus function is a [[submodular set function]]: for every two subsets ''X''<sub>1</sub>, ''X''<sub>2</sub> of ''X'':<blockquote><math>\operatorname{sur}_G(X_1\cup X_2) + \operatorname{sur}_G(X_1\cap X_2)  \leq \operatorname{sur}_G(X_1) +  \operatorname{sur}_G(X_2)</math></blockquote>A '''surplus-tight''' subset is a subset of ''X'' whose surplus equals the surplus of the entire graph (i.e., equals the minimum). The intersection and union of tight sets with non-empty intersection are tight; this follows from properties of lower-bounded submodular set functions.<ref name="lp" />{{rp|Lem.1.3.5}}

For a bipartite graph ''G'' with def(''G'';''X'') = 0, the number sur(''G'';X) is the largest integer ''s'' satisfying the following property for every vertex ''x'' in ''X'': if we add ''s'' new vertices to ''X'' and connect them to the vertices in ''N''<sub>G</sub>(''x''), the resulting graph has a non-negative surplus.<ref name="lp" />{{rp|Thm.1.3.6}}

If ''G'' is a bipartite graph with a positive surplus, such that deleting any edge from ''G'' decreases sur(''G;''X), then every vertex in ''X'' has degree sur(''G'';X)&nbsp;+&nbsp;1.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Lovász|first=L.|date=1970-09-01|title=A generalization of Kónig's theorem|journal=[[Acta Mathematica Hungarica|Acta Mathematica Academiae Scientiarum Hungaricae]]|language=en|volume=21|issue=3|pages=443–446|doi=10.1007/BF01894789|doi-access=|s2cid=121333106|issn=1588-2632}}</ref>

A bipartite graph has a positive surplus (w.r.t. ''X'') if-and-only-if it contains a forest ''F'' such that every vertex in ''X'' has degree 2 in ''F''.<ref name="lp" />{{rp|Thm.1.3.8}}

Graphs with a positive surplus play an important role in the theory of graph structures; see the [[Gallai–Edmonds decomposition]].

In a non-bipartite graph, the surplus function is, in general, not submodular.
